question: US President Donald Trump has appointed Elon Musk to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which will eradicate wasteful spending and significantly reduce the US federal budget. President Milei of Argentina has reduced the federal budget by 30 % as part of his battle against deficits.

Meanwhile, Europe’s economy is lagging strongly behind and our companies are sinking in a swamp of EU regulation and bureaucracy. The Competitiveness Compass aspires to simplify a few rules, and yet dozens of new regulations will be introduced in the coming years. Simplification and mass deregulation is needed if the EU wants to become competitive again. 1.

Can the Commission provide an overview of the concrete steps it is planning to take to accomplish mass deregulation, including a timeline of the regulations that are intended to be eliminated over time?

Over the past decades, dozens of EU decentralised agencies, joint undertakings and bodies have been created. Does the Commission intend to re-evaluate the need for and the efficiency of these undertakings, and is it willing to get rid of redundant EU agencies?

Simplification – as in the Competitiveness Compass – and deregulation will both lead to a reduction in the number of EU civil servants needed. Can the Commission provide an overview and timeline of the expected reduction in the Commission workforce, which currently consists of more than 32 800 people1?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.8.2025) 1. The President of the Commission has made the reduction of red tape a priority for the new mandate of the Commission. This includes a reduction of all burdens and a target to cut 25% of all administrative costs (35% for small and medium-sized enterprises) i.e. EUR 37.5 billion.

The Commission’s 2025 work programme contains 11 legislative measures (out of 18) which contribute to simplification, with the first five Omnibus proposals adopted in February1, May, June and July 20252. The Commission has a very ambitious simplification programme, but its proposals preserve the EU policy goals. 2.

There are currently 33 decentralised agencies partially or fully funded from the EU budget, supporting the implementation of EU policies. They are set up by the legislator on the basis of a Commission proposal, preceded by an impact assessment. In line with the Common Approach3, the founding acts of agencies require the Commission to carry out an evaluation of the agency, normally every 5 years.

The evaluation assesses the effectiveness, efficiency, coherence, relevance, and EU added value of the EU decentralised agencies4 and therefore provides a basis to decide on possible amendments to the governance or mandate of the agency and whether to continue or not its mandate. 3.

The Commission continuously strives to ensure an optimal allocation of its resources, reflecting its political priorities, legal and institutional obligations, while responding to the increasing workload generated by new and urgent needs and geopolitical crisis.

Given the new policy initiatives and the growing responsibilities assigned to the Commission by the Colegislators, the Commission looks at deploying its resources in the most efficient manner, and to continue seeking synergies and efficiencies.
